title: Friction arrival
response: Choose one route. Point, say, sign, draw or write. You may pass or say not sure. Use screen or paper; you do not need to do both.
access: For question 3, hand rubbing is optional. If comfortable, gently rub your hands for up to five seconds; stop at discomfort. You can watch an adult or describe a familiar hand-rubbing example instead. Say whether you observed it, remembered it or predicted it.
staff: Allow four minutes within the existing arrival stage. Read or scribe as needed. Start from what pupils show; the word friction is not required before it is taught. Accept uncertainty and equivalent responses. Discuss one useful observation rather than completing a second record. A remembered example or prediction is not a measurement made today.

supported.label: Supported
questions: A push moves a toy car away. Which action moved it? Push / pull.
Look at two palms pressed together. Which surfaces touch? Palm and palm / palm and sleeve.
Use your chosen route. What do you notice when hands rub? Say, point or draw one observation.
A shoe needs to grip the ground. Does grip help walking or make slipping easier? Help walking / make slipping easier.
answers: Push. Accept pointing to the word or showing the action.
Palm and palm. Accept indicating the two touching surfaces.
Accept what was actually noticed, including no noticeable warmth. A remembered or predicted change must be identified as such; do not invent an observation.
Help walking. Grip helps stop the shoe slipping against the ground.

standard.label: Standard
questions: Name the two actions that can change how an object moves: p___ and p___.
When hands rub, name the two touching surfaces.
Use your chosen route. Describe one change you notice or already know. If you know the force's name, add it.
A bike brake pad presses on the wheel rim. Predict what happens to the turning wheel.
answers: Push and pull. These are familiar ways of applying forces.
The skin of one palm and the skin of the other palm.
Accept an actual observation or a clearly identified remembered example. Hands may feel warmer. Friction is the optional force name; no noticeable warmth is also a valid observation.
The wheel slows. The pad and rim resist sliding against each other. Treat the response as a prediction unless an actual demonstration is observed.

stretch.label: Stretch
questions: A toy car is pushed, then slows on a level floor. Name one force you think could slow it. Not sure is useful.
A hand grips a door handle. Name the touching surfaces and explain what the grip helps you do.
Use your chosen route. Suggest why rubbing hands may feel warmer. Give a prediction if you cannot observe it.
Two toy cars start at different speeds on different surfaces. Is that a fair surface comparison? Name one thing to keep the same.
answers: Accept a plausible resistive force, such as friction in wheel or axle contacts or air resistance. Do not require a single location or teach that friction always opposes the whole object's travel.
Hand and handle. Grip helps turn the handle without the hand slipping over it.
Work done while rubbing transfers energy to thermal stores, so the skin may warm. Accept an initial idea to revisit; do not claim that every brief rub must produce noticeable warming.
No. Starting speeds differ as well as surfaces. Compare using the same car and a consistent release, changing the surface only; accept one sensible control.
